lesson: [lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Sharp expert-routing peaks (routing score above ~8 and several times the next expert) predicted causal single-language experts. L21 e10 (German routing 18.8) dropped en_to_de by .80 with every other skill ≤ .024, and L18 e3 (Spanish 14.1) dropped en_to_es by .665. Weak routing ranks (2–5) and mid-layer peaks were not causal: L11 e23 had code routing 72 but a 4-expert set around it dropped code by only .008. L20 e31 had Japanese routing 30 but dropped en_to_ja by only .05.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] The w2 digit-unembedding lens plus attribution agreement found arithmetic experts. L17 e7 (digit selectivity 3.4, attribution .44) dropped two_digit_addition by .342 and passed the screen, as did L17 {7,22} (.429). The strongest digit writer, L23 e14 (lens z 4.8), failed because its matched control also dropped .185, against a cap of .122.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Large attention-head groups can pass when chosen by per-layer attribution. L14 heads {5,8,10,13,18,20,23} dropped addition by .591 with control -.092. The screen ignores rises on other skills (German rose about 8×) and ignores other skills' controls. Head groups in L2, L6, L10, L18 and L21 all leaked into facts or translation; for L21 h3 it was facts .24 against a .17 cap.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Broad skills: facts localised to one L19 expert set, grown by routing while leaving out experts routed to other skills. Seed e11 gave .171, 5 experts .195, 7 experts .22, with others ≤ .063. Code never cleared .15 cleanly: L19 sets with e28 (code routing 62) topped out at .14. Math always moved together with addition (math ≤ .18), and whole-layer blocks and dense L0/L1 MLP clusters of 64–128 neurons were never selective.

[general] Do not define many overlapping narrow skills (one per language) with tiny base scores. In this run en_to_de had a base of .0004 and swung by -150 to +.8, and Romance and CJK expert sets were blocked because the sibling languages counted as other skills. Examples: L23 {2,23,24} dropped multilingual .75, but Italian .92 and Spanish .76 sank it. Prefer one family-level skill (Romance, CJK) with few-shot prompts and an English-copy control, and keep a skill slot free.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Per-layer attribution_scan (one layer at a time) plus leak-checked growth produced clean multi-expert language units. German: L21 {1,3,9,10,12,16} gave de .775 with others ≤ .122. Spanish: L22 {14,19,22} gave es .237 with others ≤ .033. French: L23 {3,9,28} gave fr .858. German also passed at L15 {3,24} (.375) and L17 {15,30} (.475). Recipe: seed with the top-attribution expert, add experts absent from sibling skills' lists, ablate after each addition, and drop any expert that leaks. Leakers were L21 e24 into es, L22 e11 into ru, L23 e22 and e5 into facts, and L18 e14, a general translation expert.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Growth saturates fast. Many added experts were inert padding with identical drops: L22 Spanish +e0/e2/e17, L18 addition +e6/e28/e31, L19 facts 8-set +e7, L23 German +e7, L22 German +e15/e26. Under routing renormalisation, adding experts can even lower the drop: L20 addition went from .164 with {1,8} to .117 with 6 experts. Stop when the drop stops rising.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] The w2 digit lens (digit-direction norm relative to the expert's other token classes, z-scored within the layer) paired with the addition-routed expert gave the cleanest arithmetic part. L18 {2,15} (writer z 2.36 plus router at routing 8.5) dropped addition .283, with math .089 and random parts ≈ 0. L17 digit experts e7/e17 always hit the digit-copy control (.15–.24 against a cap of about .14). The math built-in never moved with math-routed sets (L12 5-set, L15 6-set, L21 e23 at routing 23.8: all ≤ .016).

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Code is not separable: the L23 output experts are shared with languages. e28 is French (code routing 41.6), e27 is German (de .275 alone) and e3 is Italian (.171). The language-free code experts {7,10,20,30} drop code by only .10. L23 {3,10,27,30} reached code .188, but de .275 and it .171 sank it. Whole blocks (L22: code .388 but every translation .6–.9) and code head groups (L2, L10) were broad.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Low-base skills fail for statistical reasons, not mechanistic ones. Facts (base .0004) moves in .024 steps: L20 {6,17} was stuck at .146, and random 5-expert parts hit .244. German random parts dropped up to .7–.775. Russian, Chinese and Japanese controls (bases .008–.022) swing by -.15 to -.6 under every final-layer expert, and L21 {9,20,23} Russian (.172 on search) failed held-out. Seek a search drop of ≥ .3 and avoid skills with bases under about .05.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Dense L0/L1 MLP clusters were chaotic whether chosen by gated-embedding selectivity (128 digit units, 64 Spanish units) or by attribution. Even 8–16 units swung every translation by ±.2 to ±15. Head groups were selective only at L14: the 9-head addition group passed at .599. The L14 facts heads, and head groups in L6, L10, L18 and L21, hit all translations by .2–.9. The agent skill cap is 8, so leave slots free for broad skills.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Ranking experts by attribution within one layer and then dropping any expert that already carries another skill's collateral produced the only passing expert pool. For L20 facts, e10 (es .13, multilingual .12) and e26 (in a passed addition pool) were removed, leaving {3,6,9,17}: facts .171, other skills ≤.05, random sets ≤.07. Growing it to 5–6 experts raised facts to .195 but brought in ru .11–.12, so stop at the clean size.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Splitting a GQA key/value head group by ablation separated two skills that attribution mixed together. L18 heads 12–15 dropped math .356 and addition .622. h12/h13 carry math (.15/.17); h14+h15 drop addition .309 with math .009 and passed. Attribution ranked h11/h8 as the math heads, and those did nothing (quad .03). The margin was thin: one random 2-head set also scored .308. Every 4-head extension (adding h4/h10 or h9/h19) brought broad collateral.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] The late layers (L21–L23) hold language-family output writers, not per-language experts, so most translation pools fail single-skill screens. L23 {2,23,24} hits fr/es/it .58–.92 and multilingual .75 but not de/ru/zh/ja. L22 {11,12,13} hits all the European languages. L23 e12/e17 hit both zh and ja. Clean single-language passes came from experts with attribution for one language only: L23 e15 (es .583) and L17 e9 (es .366).

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] The down-projection digit lens and the router digit preference agreed on strong number writers (L23 e14 z5.5, router .616; L22 e31; L20 e8 number words; L19 e9 z5.2), but these are shared: L19 e9 alone hit addition .376, math .153 and the addition control .155, and L23 {14,29} hit addition .49 with control .235. Code-lens experts (L20 e26 z3.9) did nothing (code .03). Code stays near .13 per layer (L19 {28,31}), so it needs a multi-layer unit.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Skills and controls with tiny bases block screens. en_to_de_noun (base .0004) swings ±.15–.45 on unrelated ablations, and the Russian control rises as Russian is removed (L23 {13,21}: ru .978 but control −.37; L21 {9,18,20,23}: ru .332, control −.13). The Russian pool that avoided this ({9,20,23}, .172) failed held-out. Aim for search drops of at least about .25 on such skills, and define skills with high bases early, before the skill cap of 8 is used up.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Avoid early and dense parts and most head groups on this model. Clusters of 128 neurons from the L0/L1 dense layers, selected from the weights, and L2–L13 experts caused swings of .3 to −40 on the small-base skills. Head quads in L6/L10/L14/L21 were broad. L6 h21/h23 (the top facts-attribution heads) are suppressors: ablating them improves almost every skill (facts −2.6).

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Router rows dotted with token embeddings found the cleanest arithmetic experts in early layers. L5 e6 and e13 tie for the strongest digit/operator-vs-prose router preference in L5 (+.148 each). L5 e6 alone dropped two_digit_addition .231 (control .002, other skills <=.024) and passed, as did the pair {6,13} at .233. Most digit-preferring router experts elsewhere were inert or slightly negative (L6 e16, L8 {16,20}, L11 e8 at +.144, L12 {1,30}), so ablate before trusting the router signal.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Final-layer (L23) experts write tokens directly, and their output-weight SVD logit lens labels them correctly: e30 writes closing brackets, e27 code identifiers (argv, kwargs), e28 French/Spanish accented stems, e21 Russian, e12/17/29 Japanese/Chinese characters plus digits. They are rarely screenable. Language writers are shared across a family (L23 {2,23,24}: Italian .92, Spanish .76, French .58, multilingual .75). French translation is so fragile at L23 that random expert pairs dropped it .86, so L23 {28,30} (.83) failed. Define family-level skills (Romance, CJK) rather than single languages.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Code was redundant across experts and never reached the .15 threshold. The cleanest code part, L19 {28,31}, dropped code .126 with nothing else above .04. Adding router- or attribution-ranked L19 experts (15, 22/24, 9/14) stayed at about .13. Experts with high code routing frequency at L21/L22 (routing about 48) dropped code only .03, and L10 code-attributed heads dropped code .31 but damaged most other skills.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Skills that share a format block each other in screening. L19 e9 is a real arithmetic expert (math .153, addition .376), but neither skill can pass: each exceeds the other's leak limit, and addition's control also moved .155. L23 e23 dropped Italian .52 but failed because multilingual moved .192 against a .173 limit. Check every other skill against max(.05, target/3) before spending a screen.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Avoid attention head groups and dense-MLP clusters in this model. Four-head groups at L14/L18 picked by attribution moved 5-10 skills by .2-.8 each. 128-unit clusters in the dense L0/L1 MLPs, ranked either by growth from code seeds or by digit input/output alignment, produced swings of -11 to +.7 on translation skills because those skills have tiny base scores, with no selective target effect. Whole-block L19 ablation damaged everything (facts .42, Spanish .66).

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Router-row vs token-embedding alignment (gate.weight @ mean normalized category embedding) often agreed with the routing scan without being tuned to it: L14 {3,4,25} code, L12 e30 math, L22 e8 zh, L20 e31 ja. But ablating those mid-layer sets barely moved the target: code .04, math .02, zh .13, ja .14. The router tells you where a skill routes, not where it is a bottleneck.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Only final-layer (L23) experts had large effects on word-output skills. L23 {27,28} dropped en_to_fr .828 with control -.005 and passed. L23 e21 alone dropped en_to_ru .907, with other skills at .03 or less and random parts at ~0, yet failed because the ru control (base .022) moved .498. Check the control's base score before spending a skill; weak controls block even very selective parts.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] The L19 code expert set saturates: {1,28,31} gave code .128, and growing it to 5 and then 7 experts reached only .129 and .134, all clean with other skills at .03 or less. Code seems spread across layers, so one-layer expert sets stay under the .15 bar. Try blocks or multi-layer sets for code.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Large L23 expert sets are shared output hubs, not single skills. {1,12,21} hit ru .91, de .68, zh .43 and ja .30. {8,25,27,28} hit fr .86, de .60, it .24 and general_text .25. {5,29} dropped ja .26 but leaked into facts .12 and addition .10, and one random part matched it. Bisect hubs to 1-2 experts to find the selective member.

[lfm2.5_8b_a1b] Attention heads flagged by attribution in the early attention layers (L2, L6) are destructive, not skill parts. L2 {9,10,19,30,31} gave code .20 but wrecked facts (.59) and every translation skill and its control (~.9 or worse). L6 {11,22,25,26} did the same. Avoid head groups in the first attention layers of LFM2 MoE models.
